title: The Tartaro and the Talking Ring
subtitle: A short tale collected at Ahetze

ring.author: Basque storytellers; collected and translated by Wentworth Webster
ring.translator: Wentworth Webster, with assistance from Julien Vinson and other local contributors
ring.locator: THE TARTARO.; THE TARTARO., normalized characters 13-672
ring.excerpt: Once upon a time there was the son of a king who for the punishment of some fault became a monster. He could become a man again only by marrying. One day he met a young girl who refused him, because she was so frightened at him. And the Tartaro wanted to give her a ring, which she would not accept. However, he sent it her by a young man. As soon as the ring was upon her finger it began to say, "Thou there, and I here." [12] It kept always crying out this, and the Tartaro pursued her continually; and, as the young girl had such a horror of him, she cut off her finger and the ring, and threw them into a large pond, and there the Tartaro drowned himself.
ring.note: Verbatim English text from Webster's second edition, collected chiefly in Labourd. The collection distinguishes local tales from French-derived contes des fées and compares some motifs with wider European stories.

narrativeBlocks.title: A monster seeks a wife
narrativeBlocks.body: In one tale in Webster's Basque collection, a king's son becomes a Tartaro and can return to human form only by marrying.

narrativeBlocks.title: A ring will not stay silent
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (Webster's English collection; whitespace normalized): “Once upon a time there was the son of a king who for the punishment of some fault became a monster. narrativeBlocks.title: The girl escapes pursuit
narrativeBlocks.body: The frightened girl throws away the ring, but it keeps calling to the Tartaro. She finally cuts it off with her finger and throws it into a pond.

narrativeBlocks.title: A named local tale
narrativeBlocks.body: Webster says this version came from Estefanella Hirigaray of Ahetze in Labourd. It is one collected Basque story, not a universal account of every Basque community.

narrativeBlocks.title: Keep the teller attached
narrativeBlocks.body: The unusual speaking ring and the ending belong to this reported Ahetze version. Other Tartaro stories in Webster's book have different plots.
